items.title: Finite planar codes for oriented knot diagrams

references.title: Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, pp. 34–36
Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §§1.2–3.2

items.statement:
Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

items.title: A compact smooth knot has a choice-free normal tube

references.title: John Stillwell, Classical Topology and Combinatorial Group Theory, §4.2.4, Wirtinger presentation proof
Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §2

items.statement: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

items.title: A crossing-ball cover of a knot complement

references.title: John Stillwell, Classical Topology and Combinatorial Group Theory, §4.2.4, Wirtinger presentation proof
Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §2
Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §5.3, proof of the Wirtinger Presentation Proposition

items.statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Choose a sufficiently small closed normal tube $N(K)$ and set $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. If $c>0$, there is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, the Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In all cases the punctured normal tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.

items.title: Local meridian conjugacy at a Wirtinger crossing

references.title: Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, printed pp. 34–36
John Stillwell, Classical Topology and Combinatorial Group Theory, §4.2.4
Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §5.3, proof of the Wirtinger Presentation Proposition

items.statement:
Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

items.title: Removing the point at infinity preserves the knot group

references.title: Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §5.3, proof of the Wirtinger Presentation Proposition

items.statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a compact smooth knot and let $b\in\mathbb R^3\setminus K$. The inclusion $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\hookrightarrow S^3\setminus K$ induces an isomorphism
$$\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus K,b)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b).$$

items.title: Wirtinger presentation from a finite diagram code

references.title: Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §§2–3
Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, printed pp. 34–36

items.statement:
The input is a finite record $D$ and a designated starting under-arc $a_0$ of one oriented knot. First check that the vertex, edge, and segment lists are finite; that every vertex, bend, and point on an edge polyline has rational coordinates; and that each polyline has the prescribed incident endpoints. Before geometric tests, delete consecutive repeated coordinates from each polyline; reject an edge with no positive-length segment or a crossing with a zero-length incident ray. Check that every crossing has four incident half-edges, a recorded cyclic order and a pairing into alternating opposite branches, and one designated over-branch; every other vertex must be a valence-two bend. Check that edge orientations agree at bends and continue coherently through each paired branch, and that following these pairings and bends traces one oriented circle. If $a_0$ is not one of the resulting under-arcs, or any structural check fails, return invalid-input.

For every unordered pair of line segments, compute the determinant of their rational direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate intersection equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Reject every self-intersection, every positive-length overlap, and every intersection except a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence. At each crossing, sort the four nonzero incident rays by half-plane and exact determinant comparisons; reject the input if two rays have the same direction, if this geometric cyclic order disagrees with the recorded order, or if the paired branches do not alternate. These checks are finite.

After validation, traverse the oriented knot once from $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. At each crossing, let the outgoing over-half-edge be the ray in the direction of the oriented over-tangent. In the verified counterclockwise cyclic order, the under-half-edge immediately following it is the target side $a_t$; the other under-half-edge is the source side $a_s$. Read the over-arc $a_o$ and append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. This rule uses the positive in-plane normal, which points counterclockwise from the oriented over-tangent, and does not depend on the under-strand direction. The orientation of each positive meridian is fixed by requiring the oriented knot tangent followed by its normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

items.title: Correctness of the Wirtinger presentation

references.title: John Stillwell, Classical Topology and Combinatorial Group Theory, §4.2.4
Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §5.3, proof of the Wirtinger Presentation Proposition
Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram, §§2–3

items.statement: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

items.title: Explicit unknot and figure-eight oriented Wirtinger codes

references.title: Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, Lemma 5.8, printed/PDF p. 74
references.locator: The full figure-eight diagram and its Wirtinger example are context. The integer drawing, precise labels and signs used here are certified below.

items.statement:
There are the following explicit valid finite planar codes, with the standard right/up orientation of the plane and positive based meridians using compatible common upper-collar access paths.

The counterclockwise square with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ is a crossing-free unknot code. It has one under-arc and gives $\pi_1(S^3\setminus U)=\langle x\mid\ \rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with $x$ the positive meridian.

An oriented figure-eight code has crossings $C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4$. The letters $O,U$ mean over and under, and $i,o$ mean incoming and outgoing. Its integer plane-drawing certificate is

| $r$ | $C_r$ | $rOi$ | $rOo$ | $rUi$ | $rUo$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $(-423,0)$ | $(-627,102)$ | $(-363,-30)$ | $(-363,30)$ | $(-627,-102)$ |
| $2$ | $(0,-9)$ | $(-33,-6)$ | $(99,-18)$ | $(-99,-18)$ | $(33,-6)$ |
| $3$ | $(0,9)$ | $(33,6)$ | $(-99,18)$ | $(99,18)$ | $(-33,6)$ |
| $4$ | $(423,0)$ | $(627,-102)$ | $(363,30)$ | $(363,-30)$ | $(627,102)$ |

The complete cyclic visit list is $$1O,\ 2U,\ 3O,\ 1U,\ 4O,\ 3U,\ 2O,\ 4U.$$ For every successive pair $rB,sD$ in this list, including the last-to-first pair, use the three straight segments of the route $C_r\to rBo\to sDi\to C_s$. At each crossing pair $rOi$ with $rOo$, and $rUi$ with $rUo$; the first pair is over. Smooth the degree-two bends in disjoint small disks. The cyclic orders at crossings are the counterclockwise lists $(rOo,rUi,rOi,rUo)$ for $r=1,4$ and $(rOo,rUo,rOi,rUi)$ for $r=2,3$.

Label the under-arcs $x_1:U4\to U2$, $x_2:U2\to U1$, $x_3:U1\to U3$, $x_4:U3\to U4$. In each oriented over-branch chart, let $L$ denote its left under-side (target of the positive in-plane normal), and $R$ its right under-side (source). The exact crossing table is

| crossing | over | $L$ (target) | $R$ (source) | under traversal | $\operatorname{sign}\det(\text{over},\text{under})$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $R_1$ | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $x_3$ | target to source | $-1$ |
| $R_2$ | $x_4$ | $x_2$ | $x_1$ | source to target | $+1$ |
| $R_3$ | $x_2$ | $x_4$ | $x_3$ | source to target | $+1$ |
| $R_4$ | $x_3$ | $x_4$ | $x_1$ | target to source | $-1$ |

Thus its actual positive-meridian presentation is $$\pi_1(S^3\setminus 4_1)=\langle x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\mid x_1x_2=x_3x_1,\ x_1x_4=x_4x_2,\ x_3x_2=x_2x_4,\ x_3x_4=x_1x_3\rangle.$$ The last relation follows from the first three. Starting on $x_1$, the underpasses occur at $R_2,R_1,R_3,R_4$, and the self-writhe is zero. All drawing data, validations and algebra in this statement are finite and use no choice axiom.

items.title: Equal abelianizations do not classify knots

references.title: Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §§5.2–5.4, trefoil group and link group-abelianization corollary, printed pp. 68–73
Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, printed pp. 34–36

items.statement: Write $G(K):=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$ for the group of a smooth oriented knot $K$. The claim is that for every pair of such knots $K_1,K_2$, an isomorphism $G(K_1)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong G(K_2)^{\mathrm{ab}}$ implies that $K_1$ and $K_2$ are ambient isotopic.
